title: The Lord revokes commands when his servants will not act
setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, on 15 June 1831. A revelation nine days earlier had paired Thomas B. Marsh and Ezra Thayre for a mission to Missouri. Marsh was ready to leave, but Thayre was not, so Marsh asked what to do. Thayre had paid money toward the farm where he lived and may have wanted a land title first. Meanwhile the Colesville Saints at Thompson wanted Newel Knight to stay and lead their move west.
summary: The revelation opens with a warning to the rebellious among those who profess the Lord’s name. It says the Lord commands and also revokes as he sees fit. It cancels the mission of Marsh and Thayre and sends Selah J. Griffin with Marsh instead. It also cancels the mission of Griffin and Newel Knight because of rebellion at Thompson. Knight is to stay and lead the contrite there to Missouri. If Thayre repents of pride and selfishness, he may still go to Missouri; if not, he must take back his money and be cut off. If Joseph Smith must repay that money, the Lord promises to repay him in Missouri. The revelation ends with woes on selfish rich and greedy poor, and a blessing on the pure in heart.

contextNote.title: Why a command can be withdrawn
contextNote.text: Marsh needed to know whether a broken pairing still bound him. Verse 4 answers that the Lord both commands and revokes as seems good to him. Verse 3 sets the condition: cutting off comes after a command is given and broken. Verses 5–6 then apply the rule twice. Thayre’s delay ends one pairing, and the rebellion at Thompson ends another. Verse 4 places the burden “upon the heads of the rebellious,” not on those who obeyed. In this passage, to revoke means to reassign the work when people fail to act.

ldsText: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 51–57 invites readers to weigh how they use what God gives them. Verses 16–18 judge both rich and poor by the heart: what does each group lack or have?

newPeople.name: Newel Knight
newPeople.why: named in vv. 6–7; leader of the Colesville branch at Thompson, Ohio

reviewNote: Read all 20 verses. Official heading gives Kirtland, 15 June 1831, rebuking Ezra Thayre over the Frederick G. Williams farm and revoking his D&C 52 mission. JSP historical introduction (read on the /paper-summary/.../1 page) gave Marsh’s question, the 15 May revelation about Thayre, and the Thompson context. JSP says the link between Thayre’s payment and the Williams farm debt is uncertain, as is the 1871 Knight account. Williams is added because the setting requires him; he is not named in the text. Fact-check 2026-10-12: summary now states verse 9’s condition that a repentant Thayre may still go to Missouri.
